questions.question: In an interactive system development lifecycle, what does empirical evaluation assess?
options: The usability of a single prototype
The usability of the whole system
The performance of the code after testing
The appearance of the interface design
questions.explanation: Empirical evaluation, also called usability evaluation, is the evaluation of the whole system from the point of view of usability.

questions.question: At what point in the interactive system development lifecycle is empirical usability evaluation performed?
options: After every quick evaluation of a prototype
During the initial feasibility study
After the code is bug-free or runs smoothly
Before requirement gathering is complete
questions.explanation: The lifecycle places the empirical or usability evaluation stage finally, after the code is bug-free or runs smoothly.

questions.question: Why is the design, prototyping, and quick evaluation cycle repeated?
options: To refine the design until it stabilizes
To rewrite the requirements after each evaluation
To replace final usability evaluation with quick checks
To finish the full coded system as early as possible
questions.explanation: In this cycle, the design is refined based on evaluation results and repeated until the design stabilizes.

questions.question: Which stage of interactive system development is described as standard software development work with nothing special for VR or AR?
options: Quick evaluation of a design prototype
Final usability evaluation of the whole system
Repeated interface design until users are satisfied
Coding and implementation after code design
questions.explanation: Code design, coding and implementation, code testing, and code or system evaluation are standard software development stages, with nothing special or distinct for VR or AR.

questions.question: Why should cycles in the interactive system development lifecycle generally be kept infrequent?
options: To reduce the need for usability evaluation
To avoid cost and time overrun
To keep the code from being tested too early
To let the design stabilize after one pass
questions.explanation: Frequent cycles lead to cost and time overrun, so cycles should generally be kept infrequent.

questions.question: In the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, what does the term design refer to?
options: Code design and implementation architecture
Interface and interaction design
Hardware setup and content authoring planning
Requirements gathering and system specification
questions.explanation: In this cycle, design means interface and interaction design, not code design.

questions.question: Why is a quick usability evaluation needed in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle?
options: To keep many iteration cycles within a reasonable timeframe and ensure implemented design ideas become usable
To avoid creating any prototype before evaluating the final design
To replace the final empirical usability evaluation of the completed system
To measure the user's sense of presence after the system is finished
questions.explanation: Quick usability evaluation is needed so many cycles can be completed without large time or cost overrun and so design ideas lead to a usable system.

questions.question: What does the design-prototype-evaluate cycle involve before a design stabilizes?
options: Checking design guidelines, authoring assets, optimizing resources, and release
Building a prototype, writing final code, testing bugs, and measuring presence
Requirements gathering, full coding, code testing, and deployment
Designing, quick prototyping, evaluation, finding problems, refining, and repeating
questions.explanation: The cycle repeats design, quick prototyping, evaluation, problem-finding, and refinement, possibly through many cycles, before the design stabilizes.

questions.question: What is needed to evaluate a design idea quickly in the design-prototype-evaluate cycle?
options: A code design document and a resource optimization plan
A full implementation and a long-term empirical usability study
A set of design guidelines and a presence rating
A quick prototype demonstrating the idea and a quick evaluation method
questions.explanation: Quick evaluation requires both a prototype that can be built quickly and a quick method for testing that prototype.

questions.question: What are prototyping techniques mainly used for?
options: Producing a final product without later refinement or testing
Building a complete full implementation before any evaluation
Replacing design guidelines with a final verdict on usability
Quickly building and evaluating design ideas to collect usability feedback
questions.explanation: Prototyping techniques are used for quick prototyping and quick evaluation, and they are typically used to collect feedback on the usability of design ideas.

questions.question: Why can a prototype be preferred over a full implementation when testing whether a design will work?
options: It already proves the design is usable without any evaluation
It is a full implementation with similar resource, manpower, and cost demands
It implements all functionalities in depth before collecting user feedback
It is a lightweight implementation with much lower resource, manpower, and cost demands
questions.explanation: A prototype is a lightweight implementation, with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, used to test whether a design idea will work in practice.

questions.question: Why are design guidelines alone not enough to judge whether a design will work?
options: They are only a starting point and do not show whether the design is usable or unusable
They provide a quick evaluation of the design after implementation
They list the final functional requirements that guarantee a usable design
They define the user groups that must be tested in the system
questions.explanation: Design guidelines are only a starting point for a design and do not indicate whether the design is good, bad, usable, or unusable.

questions.question: What is a risk of developing a full software implementation before testing the design idea?
options: The full system is guaranteed to be usable once every function is built
Money and time spent on programmers and resources can be wasted if the idea is not good
The project avoids cost components such as resource procurement and manpower engagement
The design is accepted as good without needing empirical evaluation
questions.explanation: A full implementation involves highly skilled manpower and many cost components, so if the idea is later found not good, the money and time invested are wasted.

questions.question: What can happen to a prototype after it has been used to test design ideas?
options: It must always be replaced by a separately built full implementation
It must remain a horizontal prototype for feedback on appearance
It can be discarded, or it can be incrementally refined and tested until it becomes the final product
It cannot be changed after its first evaluation has been completed
questions.explanation: A prototype can be discarded after it has served its purpose of testing design ideas, or it can be incrementally refined and tested as development progresses until it evolves into the fully implemented final product.

questions.question: Which description best matches a horizontal prototype?
options: An in-depth implementation of selected features from first to last screen
A series of sketches showing the sequence of actions in a task
A complete implementation of every feature in the system
A surface-level depiction of the entire interface's look, feel, and appearance
questions.explanation: A horizontal prototype shows how the interface appears to the user at a surface level, without functionality or interaction.

questions.question: What is a horizontal prototype most suitable for?
options: Capturing the sequence of user actions in a task
Testing whether every feature works in the full system
Analyzing interactions implemented in selected features
Eliciting feedback about whether the interface's appearance is understandable and intuitive
questions.explanation: Horizontal prototypes are used to discuss and collect user feedback on the look, feel, and appearance of an interface.

questions.question: Which description best matches a vertical prototype?
options: An in-depth implementation of selected commonly used features, from first screen to last
A surface-level depiction of the whole interface without interaction
A single sketch showing only the layout of one screen
A complete implementation of every feature in the system
questions.explanation: A vertical prototype implements a few selected features in depth, from the first screen to the last screen after the final action.

questions.question: Why are vertical prototypes suitable for analyzing interactions and features?
options: Because they avoid implementing any functionality
Because they represent every feature in the full system
Because they implement interactions for a few selected features
Because they show the entire interface only at a surface level
questions.explanation: Vertical prototypes are suitable for analyzing interactions and features because they implement those interactions, rather than merely showing appearance.

questions.question: Which statement about the terms in a vertical prototype description is correct?
options: The term 'implemented' means building the full final system, and 'screen' means only a paper sketch
The term 'implemented' always means writing code, and 'screen' means only a physical display
The term 'implemented' means only VR rendering, and 'screen' means only a virtual scene
The term 'implemented' may not mean writing code, and 'screen' may be a 2D screen or an immersive scene
questions.explanation: In a vertical prototype, implemented and screen are generic: implementation does not require code, and a screen can be a 2D screen or a virtual or immersive scene.

questions.question: What distinguishes a low-fidelity prototype from medium- or high-fidelity prototypes?
options: It is made without a computer, code, or programming, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood.
It is made using a computer program, as reduced-scale actual software development.
It is made with digital animation or a slideshow that simulates interaction.
It is made on a computer with simple static screens, but no coding is involved.
questions.explanation: A low-fidelity prototype is created without technological intervention, programming, code, or a computer, using non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood.

questions.question: What is the primary use of low-fidelity prototyping?
options: To make a computer-based static interface or simple animation for testing interaction.
To use programming to create a reduced-scale version of the actual software system.
To make and modify prototypes quickly and cheaply, brainstorm designs, and obtain user feedback on usability.
To implement a few selected features in depth from the first screen to the last screen.
questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototyping provides a quick and cheap way to make and modify prototypes and is used primarily to brainstorm alternative designs and obtain user feedback on usability.

questions.question: How are low-fidelity prototypes related to horizontal and vertical prototypes?
options: They are used only for horizontal prototypes because they cannot represent interactions.
They are used only for vertical prototypes because they always implement functionality.
They are primarily associated with high-fidelity implementation because they require programming.
They are intuitively associated with horizontal prototypes but can also be used for vertical prototypes.
questions.explanation: Low-fidelity prototyping is intuitively primarily associated with horizontal prototyping, but it is not limited to horizontal prototypes and can also be used to implement vertical prototypes.

questions.question: What is an interface sketch?
options: A working software build that implements selected features in depth.
A hardware specification describing input devices that track user actions.
A computer-generated animation of a full interface task from beginning to end.
A simple paper drawing of major interface components, their appearance, and their layout.
questions.explanation: An interface sketch is a simple drawing, often on paper, that depicts the major components of an interface, including screen elements, buttons, selection options, their appearance, and their layout.

questions.question: How does a storyboard represent interaction in low-fidelity prototyping?
options: It uses a series of interface sketches, each a keyframe, to show user actions and screen appearances from task start to end.
It uses a single keyframe to show only the final result of the task.
It uses one detailed interface sketch to show the final appearance of the main screen.
It uses a computer program to run the complete system and test actual performance.
questions.explanation: A storyboard uses a series of interface sketches, with each sketch as a keyframe snapshot, to capture the sequence of user actions and screen appearances from the beginning of a task to its end.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes medium-fidelity prototyping from low-fidelity prototyping?
options: Medium-fidelity uses a computer without coding, while low-fidelity does not use computers or digital media.
Medium-fidelity uses programming to create reduced-scale software, while low-fidelity uses paper mockups.
Medium-fidelity uses no digital media, while low-fidelity uses simple computer animations.
Medium-fidelity relies on a hidden wizard, while low-fidelity uses static cardboard mockups.
questions.explanation: Medium-fidelity creates simple prototypes on a computer without coding, whereas low-fidelity does not rely on computers or digital media.

questions.question: What characterizes a high-fidelity prototype?
options: It uses a computer to make static sketches without any real functionality.
It relies on an unseen human operator to produce the displayed response.
It uses computer programs or programming, making it reduced-scale software development.
It is made from non-digital materials such as paper, cardboard, or wood.
questions.explanation: A high-fidelity prototype is created with computer programs or programming, so it is effectively actual software development, possibly on a reduced scale.

questions.question: Why does high-fidelity prototyping require much more effort than low- or medium-fidelity prototyping?
options: It must be built without digital tools to keep the process simple.
It only represents static screens and does not include interaction.
It is more sophisticated and needs skilled programmers with programming expertise.
It needs a hidden wizard to simulate all user responses.
questions.explanation: High-fidelity prototyping is more sophisticated and requires much more effort, including skilled programmers with programming expertise.

questions.question: In medium-fidelity prototyping, what can an animation video or a slideshow with simple key presses or timers create?
options: A low-fidelity prototype by using paper storyboards.
A vertical prototype by simulating interaction.
A full implementation by completing the entire software system.
A horizontal prototype by showing static interface sketches.
questions.explanation: In medium-fidelity prototyping, simple animated interaction can simulate a vertical prototype, while static interface sketches produce only a horizontal prototype.

questions.question: Which prototyping approach is primarily meant for vertical prototypes?
options: Medium-fidelity prototyping approaches.
High-fidelity prototyping approaches.
Hidden-wizard prototyping approaches.
Low-fidelity prototyping approaches.
questions.explanation: High-fidelity approaches are primarily meant for vertical prototypes, while low-fidelity is primarily horizontal and medium-fidelity is primarily both.

questions.question: In a Wizard of Oz prototype, who actually produces the response received by the user?
options: An unseen human operator called the wizard
The visible computer screen
A hidden camera
An autonomous computer
questions.explanation: The Wizard of Oz technique makes the user believe they are interacting with an autonomous computer, while an unseen human operator, the wizard, controls the response.

questions.question: Why was the Wizard of Oz approach used in the listening typewriter experiment?
options: To demonstrate a complete virtual reality hardware system
To test the accuracy of an existing speech recognizer
To test a speech recognition idea before the recognizer technology existed
To build a high-fidelity prototype with programmed software
questions.explanation: The approach was used to test the acceptability of a speech recognition idea before committing resources to build a recognizer, because the required technology was not yet available.

questions.question: What arrangement in the listening typewriter setup allowed the user to believe the computer was autonomous?
options: A single computer directly connected to the microphone
A hidden wizard separated from the user by a wall
A user sitting next to the hidden wizard
A wizard visible to the user through a window
questions.explanation: The setup placed a hidden wizard behind a wall, while the user faced a computer and believed it was operating on its own.

questions.question: How did the hidden wizard create the illusion that speech was automatically converted into text?
options: By having the computer convert the speech itself
By typing characters that were transmitted to the user's screen
By speaking the characters into the microphone
By having the user type the characters onto the screen
questions.explanation: The wizard heard the user's speech, typed the corresponding characters, and sent them to the user's screen, so the user believed speech had been automatically converted.

items.reason: Horizontal, vertical, and low-fidelity prototypes are kinds of prototypes; the Wizard of Oz approach is a prototype-creation technique, not a kind of prototype.

questions.question: How does the design-prototype-evaluate cycle fit into the development of an extended reality system, and why must its evaluation be quick?
questions.reference_answer: The interactive system development lifecycle is equally applicable to extended reality systems, and building interactive software is broadly similar to regular software, with differences in requirement gathering, the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, and empirical study stages. The lifecycle includes a design, prototyping, and quick evaluation cycle that is repeated until the design stabilizes, where design means interface and interaction design rather than code design. Quick usability evaluation is required because the cycle may need many repetitions; if evaluation is slow, turnaround time increases and leads to cost overrun, while a quick prototype and quick evaluation method keep the cycles within a reasonable timeframe.

questions.question: Why can a prototype be a better way to test a design idea than immediately doing a full implementation, especially when design guidelines are available?
questions.reference_answer: Design guidelines are only a starting point for a design and do not indicate whether the design is usable, so the design needs to be implemented and tested. A prototype is a lightweight implementation with much lower requirements for resources, skilled manpower, and cost than a full implementation, so it can test whether a design idea will work before programmers and expensive resources are committed. A full implementation uses highly skilled programmers and many cost components, so if the idea is later found not good, the money and time invested are wasted. After serving its purpose, the prototype can be discarded, or it can be incrementally refined and tested until it evolves into the final product.

questions.question: How do horizontal and vertical prototypes differ, and why can a storyboard support the kind of prototype that a single interface sketch cannot?
questions.reference_answer: A horizontal prototype depicts the entire interface at a surface level, showing look, feel, and appearance without functionality or interaction, so it is suitable for obtaining user feedback about appearance. A vertical prototype primarily represents selected interactions or features by implementing them in depth from the first screen to the last screen, so it is suitable for analyzing interaction. A single interface sketch is primarily a horizontal prototype because it does not show the sequence of user actions and corresponding interface changes. A series of interface sketches forms a storyboard, whose keyframes can capture the sequence of user actions from the beginning to the end of a task and thus give a vertical prototype.

questions.question: Why can the Wizard of Oz approach be useful for testing an interaction idea, and what did the IBM listening typewriter experiment use it to do?
questions.reference_answer: A prototype is used to test whether a design idea will work in practice before full implementation is committed. In the Wizard of Oz approach, a human subject believes they are interacting with an autonomous computer, but an unseen wizard operates the computer and returns the requested response. In the 1984 IBM listening typewriter experiment, the user spoke into a microphone, the hidden wizard heard the speech, typed corresponding characters, and transmitted them to the user's screen, making the user believe speech had been automatically converted. IBM used this to test the acceptability of a speech recognition system before committing resources to build one, because the automatic technology was not yet available.
